subject: Cloud Computing
title: Role-Based Access Control
description: A quick win: understand Role-Based Access Control.

hook.text: Giving every employee individual permissions doesn't scale. Fifty people, fifty unique access lists — chaos.

buildup.text: RBAC assigns permissions to roles, not individuals. You become 'Developer' or 'Admin,' and inherit that role's access.

discovery.text: When someone changes teams, you swap their role — not rewrite every permission from scratch.

twist.text: Role explosion is real. Companies end up with hundreds of roles that nobody fully understands anymore.

climax.text: Good RBAC is simple and auditable. Bad RBAC is a tangled mess that gives false confidence.

punchline.text: Roles simplify access. Too many roles recreate the mess.

quiz.question: What is 'role explosion' in RBAC?
options: Creating so many roles that the access model becomes unmanageable
A role that gives users access to every resource in the cloud
Automatically deleting all roles after a security incident

details.summary: RBAC assigns permissions to roles rather than individual users, and users are then assigned to roles. This simplifies management at scale because changing a role's permissions automatically updates access for everyone in that role.
details.whyItMatters: Managing permissions per user becomes impossible at scale. RBAC keeps access organized, auditable, and aligned with job functions across large cloud environments.
takeaways: Permissions attach to roles, not individual users
Users inherit access by being assigned to roles
Changing a role updates all members simultaneously

faq.question: How does RBAC differ from attribute-based access control?
faq.answer: RBAC assigns access based on predefined roles. ABAC evaluates attributes like user department, resource sensitivity, time of day, and location dynamically. ABAC is more flexible but more complex. Many organizations combine both approaches.

faq.question: How many roles should an organization create?
faq.answer: Create as few roles as possible while maintaining least privilege. Too many roles create management overhead. Start with broad functional roles and refine incrementally based on audit findings rather than creating a unique role for every user.
